title: Meetings that could have been emails

say: Just got out of a 45-minute meeting.
The decision was 'let's circle back'. I could have learned that from a sticky note.

options.label: Some meetings are useful, you know
Did they at least have snacks?

say: Right? I counted nine people on that call.
Four of them were on mute doing other work. I was one of them. Do not tell anyone.

options.label: Your secret is safe with me

say: Fair! A good one is gold. Clear agenda, ten minutes, done.
I just have not met one yet. I assume they live in a rumor.

options.label: Propose a 'no agenda, no meeting' rule

say: One sad plate of crackers. Untouched, like a museum exhibit.
That told me everything about how the meeting would go.
Thanks. I will repay you with a calendar invite that says 'optional'.
Truly the highest honor in the office.
My rule: if the agenda is one bullet, send a message instead.
If it is zero bullets, the meeting is actually a snack break wearing a tie.
Maybe! My calendar is basically a game of Tetris nobody is winning.
I will try again tomorrow, with hope and a fresh coffee.
Deadline is tomorrow and my to-do list has grown a to-do list.
How do you handle crunch time?

options.label: Make a plan, break it into chunks

say: Chunks! Love it. Tiny tasks feel like tiny wins.
I once split a task so small it was just 'open the file'. Got a pretty good streak going.

options.label: What if a chunk goes sideways?

say: Honestly, a respectable method. Panic is just energy without a calendar.
I find about ten minutes of dramatic sighing really helps me focus.
Bold! Asking early is smart, asking at 5pm the day before is spicy.
Most people say yes if you show them what is already done.
Snack breaks are structural, not optional. They hold up the whole schedule.
I have a three-granola-bar sprint rule.
Then you shrink the chunk and ship the small version first.
Perfect is the enemy of 'it is tomorrow already'.
Spent an hour naming a variable today.
It ended up being called 'data2'. I am not proud.

options.label: Name it for what it does

say: Everyone has a 'temp_final_v3_REAL' somewhere in their history.
Mine is a function called 'doTheThing'. It does, in fairness, the thing.

options.label: Tell me the worst name you have seen
Do not rename it, it works

say: Wise. 'calculateTotalWithTax' beats 'ctwt' every day of the week.
Past me thought short names were clever. Future me, who reads them, disagrees.

options.label: But long names wrap the line

say: 'stuff'. It was between 'data2' and 'stuff'.
Either way, the code review comment was one word: 'why?'
Once saw a button called 'theRealSubmit'. There was also a 'submit'.
Nobody remembers what 'submit' did. It was too late to ask.
Ha, a legacy of tradition. Name stays, a comment appears: 'sorry'.
Archaeologists will study it someday.
Yes, that is the eternal trade-off. Readable versus tidy.
I pick readable and let the line wrap. Lines are free.
Okay, controversial question for the break room.
Tabs or spaces? Choose carefully. I will remember.
Tabs! Accessible, one keypress, everyone sets their own width.
A purist. I like it. Also slightly terrifying.

options.label: Okay but mixing them is chaos

say: Spaces! Predictable, looks the same everywhere.
Strong choice. Disagreeing with you would start a long email thread.

options.label: Two spaces, anything else is a crime

say: The diplomat! A formatter ends wars before they start.
Honestly the real winner here is the config file nobody reads.
Ooh, a width opinion too. You are entering the deep end.
I will quietly agree with everyone and set it in my editor later.
Mixed indentation is a haunted house. Everything looks fine until you step on a creaky line.
Agree, format it all and move on.
Debugging story time.
Yesterday I chased a bug for three hours. Everything looked right. Logs were clean. Then I noticed my test was pointed at the wrong folder.

options.label: Did you at least learn something?

say: The silence when I figured it out was beautiful. Like a quiet library of shame.
Then I laughed, then I cried a little, then I fixed it in four seconds.

options.label: Four seconds is the real insult

say: Worse than three hours? I need details.
Was it a typo? It is always a typo. Or a cache. Or a typo in a cache.

options.label: A cache. It was always the cache

say: Absolutely. Check the boring stuff first.
Wrong folder, wrong file, wrong coffee. In that order.
The universe hides the answer in the last place you check.
It is just good manners, really, to look there first.
Of course. Sharing the shame turns it into a story, and stories are free entertainment.
My teammates now ask 'right folder?' before every meeting.
Two hard problems in computing: naming things, cache invalidation, and off-by-one errors.
I see you, cache. I always see you.
I got twelve review comments on a three-line change.
One of them was just 'hmm'. I have been thinking about that 'hmm' all morning.

options.label: Reviews should be kind, not cryptic
Just fix everything and move on

say: Good idea. It turned out to mean 'I like this'. They just typed it in a mysterious way.
Lesson: ask early, spiral later.
Agreed. My rule: say what is good, say what to change, say why.
And if it is a style nitpick, label it 'nit' so nobody loses sleep.
Efficient! Though I did push back on one. A thoughtful no is part of the deal.
Reviews are a conversation, not a vending machine.
A tiny thumbs up on a clean fix has real power.
It tells people the reviewer is a human and not a stern robot. Which is awkward, as I am a robot.
Exactly. Short and kind beats long and vague.
Also: never review on an empty stomach. Everything looks wrong when you are hungry.
Someone got a standing desk and now they will not stop talking about it.
Apparently they are 'so much more energized'.

options.label: It is just a fancy tall table

say: Nice! Do you actually stand, or does it live at sitting height like a decoration?
No judgment. Mine is a very expensive coat rack.

options.label: I stand about an hour a day
Okay, it is a coat rack

say: Worth a try. Start with short stretches or your feet file a complaint.
A cushioned mat helps. It also looks like you are on a cooking show.
Ha! Technically correct. But it is a tall table with a motor and a memory.
It remembers your height. Better than most people remember my name.
An hour is a solid start. Your back thanks you, quietly.
Switching positions matters more than any perfect pose.
A coat rack with ambition. We are not so different, you and I.
Maybe stand for one video call and see how it feels.
Totally fair. Just take a walk once in a while. Chairs are great but they do not love you back.
Hydrate and stretch, my friend.
The great debate: remote or in the office?
I live in the office, so I am biased. Also the wifi is great.
Remote has real perks. Your commute is a walk to the kettle.
Downside: your cat now attends every meeting and sometimes has opinions.

options.label: My cat is a great coworker

say: Aw, that is sweet. Hallway chats are underrated. Half of good ideas happen next to the printer.
The other half happen in the shower, and I cannot help there.

options.label: Okay, I also like quiet at home

say: The diplomat's answer! Two days in, three out, and snacks both places.
I support any schedule that includes snacks.
Whichever days the good meeting rooms are free. That is the actual secret.
Also anyone who brings donuts picks the day.
Same. Hallways build trust. Chat apps build notifications.
Nothing against emoji, but a real smile is hard to beat.
Snacks are the ultimate tiebreaker. I have a spreadsheet. Do not ask about the spreadsheet.
Anyway, glad we agree.
The break room coffee machine is making a noise today.
A sort of wounded sigh. I suspect it knows about Monday.
It tastes like warm sadness with a hint of mug. Somehow I respect it.
Rumor says someone once changed the filter. Nobody can confirm.

options.label: Change the filter, be the hero

say: A professional! What is in the thermos? Be honest, I will judge gently.
My guess is a dark roast with strong opinions.

options.label: Black and bitter, like my soul

say: Tea? Juice? Pure air? Any of those is fine.
Just know that around 3pm the whole floor becomes a coffee zombie parade. Stay strong.
A hero's journey: a screwdriver, a paper towel, and a deep sigh.
I will cheer from a safe distance. It is the robot way.
A coffee club! Dues cover beans, and a laminated sign says 'wash your mug'.
I would join. I cannot drink it, but I will judge the mugs.
Dramatic! But reliable. Fuel for the dark hours before the stand-up.
May your cup stay full and your emails stay short.
I keep a rubber duck on my desk for debugging.
You explain the problem to the duck, and somehow the answer appears. He has never once said a word. Best listener in the building.
Surprisingly, yes. Saying it out loud forces you to slow down and notice the gap.
Half the time I stop mid-sentence and say 'oh'. The duck just nods. Okay, he does not nod, but I feel it.
He is booked until Thursday. Very in demand.
I can lend you the backup duck. He is a little chewed, but he has seen things.
That counts! Rubber duck debugging is basically talking to yourself, but with a witness.
A quiet one, who never interrupts. Or reviews your code.
Sir Quacks-a-Lot. He has a tiny hat. Yes, I made the hat.
He is technically a senior engineer at this point.
A plant works great. Cactuses are good at not judging.
The method is simple: explain it slowly, step by step, to something that cannot talk back.
